Why waste management cannot be left to consumers alone

Consumers influence how products are used and discarded, but producers also determine packaging design, material composition, repairability and the availability of recovery systems.

When the manufacturer or other legally responsible producer bears responsibility for managing products or packaging after their use, it creates an incentive to consider these later stages during production and sale.

Extended Producer Responsibility

Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) is an environmental policy approach under which a producer's responsibility for a product extends to its post-consumer stage. Depending on the applicable rules, this may include financing or arranging collection, recycling, refurbishment or environmentally sound management.

EPR is not simply a request that producers encourage consumers to recycle. It creates defined obligations for the entities covered by a particular regulatory framework.

How an EPR system works

  1. Products are placed on the market: Producers or other covered entities manufacture, import or market the regulated products.
  2. Products or packaging become waste: Consumers, businesses and collection systems generate and collect the post-use material.
  3. Authorised recovery takes place: Appropriate collection, refurbishment or recycling activities are carried out through recognised channels, as applicable.
  4. Compliance is demonstrated: Obligated entities meet prescribed requirements using the documentation, registration, reporting or certificates required under the relevant rules.

The exact responsibilities differ among waste streams. A recycling certificate system applicable to one type of waste should not automatically be assumed to apply in exactly the same form to every other type.

Principal Indian frameworks

Waste streamPrincipal frameworkMain focus
Plastic packagingPlastic Waste Management Rules, 2016, as amended; EPR guidelines introduced in 2022Producer responsibility for regulated plastic packaging waste
Electronic wasteE-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022Producer obligations and environmentally sound handling of covered electrical and electronic waste
Waste batteriesBattery Waste Management Rules, 2022Producer responsibility for covered batteries, including collection and recycling or refurbishment

Plastic packaging

Plastic packaging EPR operates within the framework of the Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016, as amended. EPR guidelines for plastic packaging were introduced in 2022.

Producers, importers and brand owners may have obligations concerning the packaging they place on the market, according to the applicable provisions. The details of collection, recycling, reuse and end-of-life treatment depend on the relevant packaging category and the rules in force.

Plastic waste management involves more than collecting a large quantity of plastic. Actual recycling, suitable recovery and prevention of environmental leakage matter. Mixed or contaminated plastic can be difficult to process safely.

Electronic waste

The E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022 were notified on 2 November 2022 and came into force on 1 April 2023, replacing the earlier 2016 rules for matters governed by the new framework.

The framework covers specified electrical and electronic equipment and provides for producer responsibility and regulated recovery activities. E-waste can contain valuable metals and recoverable components, but unsafe processing may expose workers and the environment to hazardous substances.

Consequently, circularity in electronics involves both extending product life and ensuring that end-of-life materials are processed through environmentally sound channels.

Waste batteries

The Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022 provide a framework based on EPR for covered batteries. The rules address portable, automotive, industrial and electric-vehicle batteries.

They place responsibilities on producers, including importers, for management of waste batteries through collection and recycling or refurbishment, as applicable. Batteries contain materials that may be recoverable but can also create environmental and safety risks when improperly handled.

Principal institutions and responsibilities

  • Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC): The Union ministry responsible for the central environmental policy and regulatory framework, including the principal waste-management rules discussed here.
  • Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB): The central pollution-control institution involved in implementing and monitoring relevant environmental and waste-management requirements, including designated EPR systems.
  • State Pollution Control Boards: State-level bodies with responsibilities under applicable environmental laws and rules. In Gujarat, the relevant institution is the Gujarat Pollution Control Board (GPCB).
  • Producers and registered recovery entities: Businesses that must meet their respective obligations under the rules applicable to the products or waste they handle.

Regulatory bodies establish or supervise compliance systems; they are not necessarily the organisations that physically collect and recycle every discarded product.

Waste prevention, collection and recycling must work together

EPR improves accountability for post-consumer waste, but it does not replace the need to prevent unnecessary waste. A durable and repairable electronic product may require fewer replacements. Proper waste segregation can improve recovery quality. Safe processing prevents hazardous material from becoming a new source of pollution.

These measures form a connected system: producers improve products and accept defined responsibilities, consumers use and segregate goods responsibly, recovery enterprises manage materials, and regulators oversee compliance.

Reading regulations with the correct date

Waste-management rules may be amended after their initial notification. The 2016, 2022 and 2024 years associated with major Indian frameworks identify their original schemes or rules, not necessarily the complete requirements applicable in every later year.

At the 1 November 2026 content cutoff, the EPR framework should be understood through the relevant principal rules together with amendments in force by that date. Numerical recycling targets, reporting requirements and registration procedures should not be assumed to remain unchanged merely because the title of the principal rules remains the same.

Prelims focus

  • EPR extends producer responsibility to the post-consumer stage of covered products or packaging.
  • Plastic packaging EPR operates under the Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016, as amended, with EPR guidelines introduced in 2022.
  • The E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022, came into force on 1 April 2023.
  • The Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022, cover portable, automotive, industrial and electric-vehicle batteries.
  • CPCB is a central institution; GPCB is Gujarat's State Pollution Control Board.
  • Trap: EPR does not mean producers are automatically required to collect every discarded item personally; their obligations follow the applicable rules and compliance system.

[Sources: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, 'Rules and Regulations', entries for Plastic Waste Management Rules, E-Waste (Management) Rules and Battery Waste Management Rules, including listed amendments, consulted 1 November 2026; Government of India, E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022, Rules 1–2 and provisions on extended producer responsibility; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, 'Government notifies Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022', 25 August 2022, Release ID 1854433; Press Information Bureau, 'Parliament Question: Circular Economy Framework and Extended Producer Responsibility', 23 March 2026, Release ID 2244104; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 16, 'Environmental Issues', section 16.3, 'Solid Wastes'.]
